notes: PROPERTY BOUGHT IN A SCENARIO IS NOW SOMETHING YOU OWN, with the loan still owed shown against it. THE GAP, MEASURED FIRST: a house or land scenario produced exactly two rows, both of kind 'expense' — a down payment in one month and an EMI across the tenure. No asset was ever created and no liability either. A Rs 1 crore plot bought in April 2031 with 20% down over 20 years at 8.5% left net worth Rs 2,82,53,683 lower at the final EMI, having absorbed Rs 1.87 crore of payments and credited nothing. The gap also kept WIDENING after the loan ended — another Rs 61 lakh over five further years with no payments at all — because the cash spent was still being charged its lost compounding while the thing it bought stayed invisible. For land and houses, where the asset is the entire point, the section could state what a purchase costs and was structurally unable to state what it gains. WHAT WAS BUILT: two new series on scenario effects, assetDelta and liabDelta, both folded into net worth. BOTH are required and shipping either alone would be worse than shipping neither — the asset without the debt would lift net worth by the whole borrowed sum on day one, a larger error than the original and in the flattering direction. The asset starts at purchase cost and compounds monthly at a rate the user sets; the liability is the loan amortised month by month from the real EMI and rate, stored negative to match liabSeries. THE INVARIANT THAT PROVES IT: a leveraged purchase should move net worth by almost nothing on the day it happens, since asset up and debt up very nearly cancel. Measured day-one change is minus Rs 56,667, which is precisely one month's interest on Rs 80 lakh at 8.5%. That is the correct answer rather than an approximation of it: interest is a genuine loss, principal merely converts cash into equity. VERIFIED ACROSS THE WHOLE TENURE on the same Rs 1 crore example at 6% growth: purchase minus Rs 56,667; five years minus Rs 4.52 lakh; ten years minus Rs 2.86 lakh; final EMI PLUS Rs 36.62 lakh with the asset at Rs 3.19 crore and nothing owed; five years later plus Rs 85.76 lakh. Two controls confirm the wiring — at 0% growth the position is exactly Rs 1 crore better than before, the asset held at cost and nothing more; with the toggle off the result is minus Rs 2,82,53,683, identical to the old behaviour to the rupee. DEFAULTS AND CONTROLS: houses and land default to owned, cars and 'other' do not, matching the user's decision to ignore cars entirely rather than model depreciation. The default growth rate is 6% a year, editable per scenario, and the toggle can override the default either way. The growth field only appears when the purchase is kept. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED FROM LIQUIDITY: the asset is not added to the Decisions liquidity test. Land is illiquid by definition, and counting it would mean buying land made the emergency-cover test EASIER to pass, so a car decision could start passing because a plot was bought. NOT MODELLED, AND SAID SO IN THE UI: stamp duty and registration, roughly 6-7% in Karnataka, are not deducted. The growth field carries a note that the figure is the user's assumption rather than a forecast and that those costs are never recovered. Net worth is rebuilt in three separate places in the engine; all three now add these series, so the post-processing passes cannot silently drop them. Regression confirms the Projection-to-Dashboard and Decisions-to-chain gaps both remain zero. No page errors.
